taxonomy.title: General-surgeon essentials — nerves and orthopedics
taxonomy.scopeIn: Nontraumatic peripheral nerve localization, postoperative nerve injury outside a specific operative-family objective, musculoskeletal mimics and urgent orthopedic infection essentials.
taxonomy.scopeOut: Traumatic head/spine/extremity care belongs to trauma-head-spine-extremities. Hernia-specific pain belongs to hernia-groin. Thyroid laryngeal injury stays in thyroid-nodules-cancer.
taxonomy.priorityReason: A small essentials lane keeps adjacent-specialty objectives explicit and bounded.
researchAgenda: Urgent bone/joint infection or compression recognition
taxonomy.coverageReason: At most four distinct live clinical concept identities cover this scope. Variants repeat those identities.
taxonomy.testingWeightBasis: Owner-directed editorial estimate of general-surgery testing relevance. No exam percentages or official blueprint weights are asserted.

A deltoid-focused deficit does not explain medial winging on forward pushing.

nodes.task: Which next study best resolves whether the outside conduction result supports an intervention for {patientName}'s hand symptoms?

choices.label: Temperature-controlled median and control-nerve conduction studies
choices.rationale: The sensory map makes a distal median process plausible, but this isolated absolute measurement is confounded. A controlled comparative acquisition can establish whether focal slowing is real.
choices.temptation: Accept the report's abnormal label as sufficient confirmation for an intervention.
choices.counterfactual: If the available study already contained adequate concordant comparative measurements, this technical repeat would not be the best next step.

choices.label: Needle EMG of cervical paraspinal and proximal arm muscles
choices.rationale: The old foraminal image is a plausible competing explanation, but the current distribution does not supply proximal findings that outweigh the unresolved distal measurement.
choices.temptation: Anchor on a structural cervical abnormality while treating the distal study as already validated.
choices.counterfactual: New radiating arm pain and weakness outside distal median muscles would make a proximal localization study relevant.

choices.label: Ultrasound of the median nerve and flexor tendons
choices.rationale: Anatomic ultrasound can address a structural wrist question, but it does not determine whether this temperature-sensitive physiological result demonstrates focal conduction slowing.
choices.temptation: Substitute an anatomic image for checking the validity of the physiological evidence being used to justify treatment.
choices.counterfactual: A concordant valid physiological study plus unexplained focal fullness would create a structural imaging question.

nodes.explanation: The symptoms and the acquisition must be interpreted separately. This record supports considering a distal median process but does not yet supply an adequately controlled physiological confirmation. The key corrects this particular confounder; it does not mean every cold-hand study is uninterpretable or that symptoms alone mandate surgery.
reasoningSteps: Localize the sensory complaint while resisting attribution to the older cervical image.
Identify the confounder in an isolated absolute latency and choose an acquisition that resolves it before intervention.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Use the old foraminal MRI to redirect testing without first resolving the technically uncertain distal result.
nodes.decidingObservation: Only an isolated absolute latency from a cold hand supports the reported distal abnormality; the clinical distribution lacks the proximal findings that would favor the root study.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Replace the sensory-only distal pattern with radiating neck-to-arm pain and weakness in several nonmedian proximal muscles: the root-directed needle study becomes the relevant localization plan.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete the acquisition details and the reason for a controlled repeat disappears. Delete the distribution and proximal examination and root-directed testing cannot be ranked. The older image creates the actual anchoring competitor. The numeric temperature is a fictional measurement, not an authored diagnostic cutoff.

nodes.task: Which referral plan should lead treatment of {patientName}'s progressive hand motor loss?

choices.label: Hand-surgical assessment for carpal tunnel release

choices.temptation: Judge treatment success from sensory relief while overlooking deteriorating motor function.
choices.counterfactual: Improved sensation with stable strength and no progressive wasting could support continued nonsurgical follow-up.

choices.label: Spine-surgical assessment for cervical root decompression
choices.rationale: The cervical image is a real competing record, but it is less concordant with the selective distal physiology and thenar deficit than the hand-level findings.
choices.temptation: Attribute all hand weakness to an abnormal cervical image despite more concordant distal evidence.
choices.counterfactual: Weakness extending into nonmedian proximal muscles with root-concordant findings would shift priority toward cervical evaluation.

choices.label: Hand-therapy review for continued conservative symptom care
choices.rationale: Sensory improvement makes this tempting, but continued motor deterioration means symptom relief has not resolved the consequential deficit.
choices.temptation: Use improvement in tingling as the sole measure of adequate response.
choices.counterfactual: Sustained symptom improvement with preserved strength and no progressive atrophy would make conservative symptom care more appropriate.

nodes.explanation: Palmar abduction is specified so the observed deficit is not confused with thumb extension. The current motor trajectory and focal physiology outweigh sensory improvement and an uncorrelated cervical image for this referral decision. This is an assessment for release, not a rule that an old MRI excludes coexisting root disease.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the precise motor action and selective conduction pattern as distal median dysfunction rather than thumb-extension or generalized root weakness.
Use progressive motor loss, rather than sensory relief, to prioritize hand-surgical assessment.

nodes.deletionTest: The movement direction prevents ambiguity with extension or radial abduction. The focal comparative physiology and proximal sampling distinguish the cervical competitor. Removing the differing motor and sensory trends removes the management conflict. Neither conservative option is a verbatim failed repeat.

nodes.objective: Recognize when an apparent elbow neuropathy cannot explain a wider neurologic pattern and redirect the next investigation.

items.label: Current hand findings
items.value: Fine finger movements are now slow in both hands, including thumb-index tasks; the patient drops small objects despite the sensory improvement.

items.label: Current walking examination

nodes.task: Which investigation should lead evaluation of {patientName}'s worsening hand function and walking difficulty?

choices.label: MRI of the cervical spine
choices.rationale: Bilateral hand dysfunction plus upper motor neuron and gait findings cannot be explained by the focal elbow result; cervical cord assessment addresses the broader pattern.
choices.temptation: Let a genuine mild elbow abnormality explain every later symptom.
choices.counterfactual: A purely unilateral ulnar sensory/motor deficit without gait or upper motor neuron findings would keep the local nerve pathway in the foreground.

choices.label: MRI of the right brachial plexus
choices.rationale: A postoperative arm problem can prompt plexus imaging, but a unilateral plexus lesion does not account for the bilateral hand and leg findings.
choices.temptation: Infer a larger peripheral injury from the postoperative timing without localizing the whole examination.
choices.counterfactual: Weakness across several nerves in one arm with a matching peripheral distribution and no leg signs would make plexus assessment more relevant.

choices.label: MRI of the right elbow
choices.rationale: The local study and initial paresthesia make this plausible, but a local elbow image will not resolve the new bilateral and lower-limb pattern.
choices.temptation: Keep escalating local imaging because the first abnormal test was at the elbow.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent focal elbow symptoms with a local mass or other unresolved structural finding would make elbow imaging a relevant next inquiry.

nodes.explanation: The initial focal finding need not be false to be insufficient. The resident must localize the newly broader examination before choosing imaging: hand dysfunction with gait and upper motor neuron findings raises a cervical cord concern. No diagnosis or operative technique is established before imaging.
reasoningSteps: Determine that the distribution and long-tract findings extend beyond an isolated postoperative ulnar or unilateral plexus deficit.
Select cervical MRI to assess the cord rather than continue local arm imaging.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Continue elbow imaging because an earlier physiological abnormality genuinely involved that region.

nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Replace the bilateral hand and leg findings with persistent unilateral little/ring-finger symptoms and a focal elbow fullness: local elbow imaging becomes relevant, and the basis for cervical cord priority disappears.
nodes.deletionTest: The initial genuine focal result creates the anchoring error and the actual sensory response prevents calling it a failed local treatment. Bilateral hand involvement and the walking/reflex findings establish a different localization. Removing those findings eliminates the reason to prioritize cervical over peripheral imaging.

nodes.task: Which management plan best fits {patientName}'s current elbow and hand findings?

choices.label: Refer for right cubital-tunnel surgical assessment
choices.rationale: The right motor trajectory and concordant physiology justify escalation despite sensory improvement; bilateral mobility does not establish bilateral symptomatic disease.
choices.temptation: Choose treatment intensity and side from an image instead of the functional deficit.
choices.counterfactual: If right strength and function were preserved and symptoms continued to settle, protective care could remain appropriate.

choices.rationale: This fits the sensory improvement but underweights progressive objective right motor loss and muscle wasting.
choices.temptation: Define success by less tingling while ignoring worsening intrinsic function.
choices.counterfactual: Improving paresthesia with stable normal power and no progressive muscle loss would favor continued protective care.

choices.label: Refer for bilateral cubital-tunnel surgical assessment
choices.rationale: The ultrasound shows mobility on both sides, but the left side has no clinical or physiological neuropathy to justify the same escalation.
choices.temptation: Treat bilateral sonographic mobility as bilateral disease requiring equivalent intervention.
choices.counterfactual: Bilateral concordant symptoms, objective deficits and nonresponse would justify assessing both sides rather than inferring disease from mobility alone.

nodes.explanation: The current decision concerns progressive right motor dysfunction, not obtaining a dynamic image. Less tingling does not reverse the recorded weakness. reasoningSteps: Reconcile improving sensory symptoms with worsening right intrinsic motor function and focal physiology.
Escalate the affected side while recognizing that the same ultrasound movement on an asymptomatic side does not establish equal disease.

choices.counterfactual: Known transection, deterioration or a persistently nonrecovering lesion would change the specialist exploration question.

choices.label: Refer for scapular tendon-transfer reconstruction
choices.rationale: A fixed persistent deficit may eventually create a reconstruction question, but this record documents improving neural and functional performance.

choices.counterfactual: A lasting disabling nonrecovering deficit after specialist evaluation and rehabilitation could make reconstructive assessment relevant.

nodes.task: Which ultrasound-guided aspiration plan best addresses the unresolved cause of {patientName}'s painful native knee?

choices.label: Lateral suprapatellar entry into the joint
choices.rationale: The first sample does not establish the contents of the joint. This route obtains joint fluid while avoiding the inflamed superficial anterior pocket.
choices.temptation: Accept a specimen label and its crystals as proof that the intra-articular compartment has been evaluated.
choices.counterfactual: If an adequate intra-articular sample already existed and there were no remaining joint concern, repeating joint aspiration would require a new reason.

choices.label: Anterior entry through the pocket into the joint
choices.rationale: This would reach the relevant deeper compartment but traverse the overlying inflamed collection, creating an avoidable contamination or inoculation concern.
choices.temptation: Correct the target compartment without considering the access route.
choices.counterfactual: An anterior approach through uninflamed tissue without an intervening collection can be an acceptable joint access route.

choices.label: Anterior entry into the prepatellar pocket
choices.rationale: The pocket may need evaluation in its own right, but its fluid will still not represent the separate joint effusion responsible for the unresolved intra-articular concern.
choices.temptation: Treat the superficial crystal-containing collection as the complete explanation for the painful knee.
choices.counterfactual: A purely superficial process without a joint effusion or pain on passive joint motion would make the superficial pocket the relevant local target.

nodes.explanation: A label does not replace specimen provenance. The images show what was sampled; crystals and a negative stain in that fluid do not settle the separate joint question. The new sample must reach the joint through an appropriate route. This sampling decision does not suspend needed systemic treatment or establish that every superficial collection communicates with the joint.
reasoningSteps: Infer from needle position that the crystal-containing sample did not represent the separate joint effusion, leaving the joint concern unresolved.
Choose access to the joint that avoids traversing the inflamed superficial collection.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Use an anterior route that reaches the joint but crosses the superficial pocket.
nodes.decidingObservation: The documented needle tip is superficial to the patella, while a separate joint effusion and passive-motion pain remain; the anterior route crosses the inflamed pocket.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If the anterior skin and path were uninflamed with no intervening collection, anterior entry could be reasonable. If the painful process were confined to a superficial pocket without effusion or passive-motion pain, the pocket would become the local aspiration target.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete the actual tip location and the first aspirate's scope cannot be judged. Delete the separate effusion and passive-motion pain and the need for joint sampling weakens. Delete the overlying collection and skin findings and the lateral-versus-anterior route cannot be ranked. The crystal result remains a genuine misleading attribution, not a diagnosis label.

authorGate.coverTheKey: All options are ultrasound-guided aspiration routes, with identical timing metadata. None abandons antibiotics or offers steroid injection. The closest competitor reaches the same joint, so the learner must interpret both sample provenance and access anatomy rather than choose the only infection-preserving treatment.
authorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three local aspiration routes at the same diagnostic sampling stage.
twoConsequentialSteps: Infer from needle position that the crystal-containing sample did not represent the separate joint effusion, leaving the joint concern unresolved.
Choose access to the joint that avoids traversing the inflamed superficial collection.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate prediction: two linked anatomy/provenance decisions replace the single crystals-do-not-exclude-infection rule. No easy-item exception or independent PASS is claimed.
authorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: The documented needle tip is superficial to the patella, while a separate joint effusion and passive-motion pain remain; the anterior route crosses the inflamed pocket. Counterfactual re-solved: If the anterior skin and path were uninflamed with no intervening collection, anterior entry could be reasonable. If the painful process were confined to a superficial pocket without effusion or passive-motion pain, the pocket would become the local aspiration target.

New procedure images show that the reported crystals came from a different compartment; the label cannot establish joint sampling adequacy. Added actual skin/path observations that make the nearest competing joint-entry route less appropriate, supported by SANJO aspiration guidance. Crystals and negative Gram stain are limited to the sampled fluid; no statement suspends needed antimicrobial or source-control care. All choices re-solved from the visible standalone context; this is an author check, not independent approval.

items.value: The laboratory received a small amount of newly aspirated fluid and reported that it could not perform every requested test.

nodes.task: Which requested analysis should receive priority for {patientName}'s limited repeat knee aspirate?

choices.label: Bacterial culture of the new aspirate
choices.rationale: Bacterial identification remains the priority when volume is limited. A PCR detection has not provided a viable isolate for standard susceptibility testing.
choices.temptation: Do not consider microbiology complete merely because one organism-directed assay was positive.
choices.counterfactual: If culture material were already adequately secured and the remaining problem were crystal identification, microscopy could receive the residual sample.

choices.label: Leukocyte count of the new aspirate
choices.rationale: A numerical inflammatory count cannot substitute for bacterial identification in this unresolved culture workup.
choices.temptation: Prioritize the familiar inflammatory cutoff rather than a recoverable organism.
choices.counterfactual: After sufficient microbiology sampling, count/differential can add useful inflammatory context.

choices.label: Crystal microscopy of the new aspirate
choices.rationale: Crystals could coexist with infection and should not displace bacterial identification when fluid is scarce.
choices.temptation: Treat a possible crystal explanation as more actionable than culture after a positive molecular result.
choices.counterfactual: If microbiologic needs were already met and the residual clinical question were crystal arthritis, this would become relevant.

nodes.explanation: Use scarce synovial material to preserve bacterial identification first. The positive molecular result does not create a cultured isolate, and an inflammatory count or crystal result cannot replace it.
reasoningSteps: Recognize that organism DNA detection and recovery of a viable culture isolate are different outputs.
Prioritize bacterial culture over inflammatory characterization when the new sample cannot support all requested tests.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Sending the scarce sample for another inflammatory number after assuming PCR finished the microbiology.
nodes.decidingObservation: PCR is positive but there is no culture isolate, and the new specimen is inadequate for every analysis.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: With microbiology already adequately sampled and only a residual crystal question, crystal microscopy could take priority on remaining material.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete sample scarcity and all tests can be appropriate; the single-priority task would be artificial. Delete the no-isolate observation and the workup stage is unclear.

items.value: The hospital performed an arthroscopic washout of an infected native knee and started antibiotics active against the recovered organism.

items.label: Interval findings

nodes.task: Which next treatment step best fit {patientName}'s knee at this recorded reassessment?

choices.label: Repeat arthroscopic knee debridement
choices.rationale: Persistent purulence, deteriorating function and rising inflammatory markers support failed source control despite an active antimicrobial regimen.
choices.temptation: Separate antimicrobial susceptibility from whether infected material has been adequately cleared.
choices.counterfactual: A dry improving knee with falling inflammatory markers would favor continuing treatment rather than repeat debridement.

choices.label: Change to broader intravenous antibiotics
choices.rationale: The available susceptibility and administration record do not identify inadequate antimicrobial activity; the local purulent course requires renewed source-control attention.
choices.temptation: Explain every treatment failure as an insufficiently broad drug spectrum.
choices.counterfactual: A new resistant isolate or documented inadequate antimicrobial activity could warrant a regimen change.

choices.label: Continue the current intravenous antibiotics
choices.rationale: Passive continuation overlooks combined evidence of local treatment failure.
choices.temptation: Assume that an active drug necessarily compensates for residual infected material.
choices.counterfactual: Improving pain, a dry wound and decreasing markers would support the existing plan.

nodes.explanation: An active antibiotic does not establish adequate source control. The combined local deterioration and inflammatory trend support repeat orthopedic debridement assessment, without claiming that any single CRP value mandates surgery.
reasoningSteps: Integrate persistent purulence, worsening joint function and inflammatory trajectory as failure rather than expected discomfort.
Use verified active therapy to prioritize renewed source control over an automatic spectrum change or passive continuation.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Broadening an already active antimicrobial regimen while infected joint material remains uncontrolled.
nodes.decidingObservation: Purulence and reaccumulation persist as function worsens despite documented active therapy.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If the knee were dry and improving with falling markers, continuing the current therapy would outrank another washout.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete local purulence and rising CRP alone would not establish the same surgical priority. Delete susceptibility/administration evidence and inadequate drug delivery remains a competing explanation.

nodes.objective: Select immediate local compression assessment from evolving postoperative limb findings after block resolution.
nodes.currentUpdate: The clinic review reaches the outside postoperative assessment after the repeat knee washout; the question concerns what that hospital team needed to assess immediately.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Block and motor course
items.value: The regional block had resolved with initially documented ankle movement. Later examinations showed progressively weaker ankle dorsiflexion and toe movement.

items.label: Local findings
items.value: Deep calf pain rose despite analgesia. The calf became swollen and firm, and passive toe movement markedly increased pain.

items.label: Perfusion
items.value: The foot remained warm with palpable pedal pulses.

nodes.task: Which immediate evaluation should lead the outside team's response to {patientName}'s worsening postoperative leg findings?

choices.label: Immediate surgical assessment of calf compartments
choices.rationale: The progressive deep pain, stretch pain, firmness and evolving motor deficit require bedside assessment for treatable local pressure despite preserved pulses.
choices.temptation: Use a warm foot and pulses to exclude a pressure problem or route the weakness directly to delayed nerve testing.
choices.counterfactual: Soft painless compartments with an isolated stable nerve-territory deficit would favor a peripheral-nerve localization assessment.

choices.label: Immediate venous assessment with leg duplex ultrasound
choices.rationale: Postoperative swelling makes venous thrombosis a credible concern, but duplex does not resolve the combined stretch pain, firmness and worsening motor deficit that need direct compartment assessment.
choices.temptation: Attribute painful postoperative swelling to venous obstruction while underweighting the evolving local neuromuscular findings.
choices.counterfactual: Swelling and venous tenderness without compartment firmness, stretch pain or neurologic progression would make venous investigation more appropriate.

choices.label: Immediate peripheral-nerve assessment with electrodiagnosis
choices.rationale: Progressive weakness deserves specialist attention, but physiology is not the first way to exclude a surgically treatable local pressure problem in this painful swollen limb.
choices.temptation: Assume every post-block motor deficit should first be classified by nerve conduction or EMG.
choices.counterfactual: A persisting localized deficit after reversible compression is excluded, with a soft painless limb, would make electrodiagnostic localization useful.

nodes.explanation: The deficit appeared after block resolution and is progressing with local pain and swelling. Palpable pulses assess arterial flow but do not exclude a compartment pressure problem. Surgical bedside assessment must address reversible compression; pressure measurement may assist when indicated. The draft neither diagnoses a specific mechanism from timing nor substitutes consultation for examining the limb.
reasoningSteps: Interpret the serial motor loss with local stretch pain and firmness as a possible treatable pressure complication rather than residual block or an isolated physiological nerve problem.
Prioritize immediate compartment-focused surgical assessment over other urgent but less relevant investigations.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Obtain venous duplex first because postoperative pain and swelling suggest thrombosis.
nodes.decidingObservation: Progressive motor loss occurs with a firm calf and pain on passive stretch, despite a warm foot and palpable pulses.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Replace the firm, stretch-painful limb and progressive motor deficit with soft compartments, normal power and predominantly venous swelling/tenderness: urgent venous duplex becomes the more relevant investigation.
nodes.deletionTest: Block resolution and initially present movement establish a new progressive deficit. Local pain, stretch pain and firmness select the assessment pathway; preserved pulses create a real false-reassurance competitor. The old early-normal EDX detail was removed because it did not change urgency or test ranking. All proposed paths remain immediate.

twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret the serial motor loss with local stretch pain and firmness as a possible treatable pressure complication rather than residual block or an isolated physiological nerve problem.
Prioritize immediate compartment-focused surgical assessment over other urgent but less relevant investigations.

Counterfactual re-solved: Replace the firm, stretch-painful limb and progressive motor deficit with soft compartments, normal power and predominantly venous swelling/tenderness: urgent venous duplex becomes the more relevant investigation.

nodes.objective: Investigate inflammatory back pain despite an afebrile examination and degenerative plain films.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Symptoms
items.value: Focal lumbar pain persisted at rest and repeatedly woke the patient from sleep.

items.label: Outside evaluation
items.value: The patient was afebrile, with unchanged leg strength and sensation. CRP remained above the laboratory reference range.

items.label: Existing imaging
items.value: Lumbar radiographs showed osteophytes and disc-space narrowing without an acute fracture; no cross-sectional spine imaging had been performed.

nodes.task: Which next spine study best fit {patientName}'s initial outside evaluation?

choices.label: Contrast-enhanced lumbar spine MRI
choices.rationale: The infection history and inflammatory course remain concerning despite absent fever and degenerative radiographs. MRI evaluates early vertebral/disc and adjacent soft-tissue infection.
choices.temptation: Do not let common degenerative findings close a question they have not assessed.
choices.counterfactual: A genuine MRI contraindication requires an alternative imaging strategy for the same diagnostic goal.

choices.label: Noncontrast lumbar spine CT
choices.rationale: CT is useful for bony detail but is not the preferred next assessment of this suspected disc/soft-tissue process when MRI is feasible.
choices.temptation: Choose bone detail rather than the modality needed for this clinical question.
choices.counterfactual: Bony destruction or stabilization planning after infection localization can make CT useful.

choices.label: Technetium lumbar bone scan
choices.rationale: A bone scan is not preferred when MRI can assess the vertebral and adjacent soft-tissue process.
choices.temptation: Use a general bone-turnover test instead of matching the diagnostic target.
choices.counterfactual: A real MRI contraindication can justify a selected alternative imaging strategy.

nodes.explanation: Afebrile status and degenerative films do not adequately explain persistent focal pain with continuing inflammatory evidence. MRI addresses the vertebral/disc and adjacent soft-tissue question.
reasoningSteps: Integrate rest/night pain and persistent inflammatory evidence rather than anchor on degeneration.
Select imaging that evaluates the suspected vertebral/disc and adjacent soft-tissue process.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Attributing the whole presentation to common degenerative findings because fever is absent.
nodes.decidingObservation: Focal rest/night pain and elevated CRP persist while the available study is a degenerative plain film.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If infection were already localized and the immediate question became cortical bone destruction for stabilization planning, CT would become the appropriate imaging target.
nodes.deletionTest: Delete the inflammatory pain course and CRP evidence and degeneration may be a sufficient explanation. Delete the prior imaging type and retrieval rather than a new scan could be appropriate. No prior bloodstream isolate is assumed or supplied.

authorGate.coverTheKey: Three named imaging studies have existing timing profiles. The task does not say infection, gold standard or sensitive. The neurologic examination establishes the present care phase rather than excluding infection.
authorGate.sameDecisionStageAndCategory: Three next diagnostic spine imaging studies.
twoConsequentialSteps: Integrate rest/night pain and persistent inflammatory evidence rather than anchor on degeneration.
Select imaging that evaluates the suspected vertebral/disc and adjacent soft-tissue process.

authorGate.singleDefensibleBestAnswer: Focal rest/night pain and elevated CRP persist while the available study is a degenerative plain film. If the question instead concerned cortical destruction after infection localization for operative planning, CT would become useful.

nodes.task: Which initial sampling and treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s current spinal record? In these plans, treatment after sampling means after specimen acquisition, not after final culture results.

choices.label: Image-guided disc/endplate sampling before starting empiric antibiotics
choices.rationale: Stable physiology and neurology allow initial microbiologic/histologic tissue acquisition. Without an operative indication, image-guided sampling is the less invasive initial diagnostic route.
choices.temptation: Treat acquisition and final laboratory results as the same boundary or infer an operation from the MRI label.
choices.counterfactual: New sepsis or neurologic deterioration would change whether treatment and operative assessment can wait for this diagnostic sequence.

choices.label: Empiric antibiotics before obtaining image-guided disc/endplate samples
choices.rationale: The acquisition route is reasonable, but in this untreated stable record it gives up the opportunity to obtain tissue before antimicrobial exposure.
choices.temptation: Treat MRI suspicion as requiring antimicrobial administration before available diagnostic sampling in every stable patient.
choices.counterfactual: Hemodynamic instability or an unsafe delay to sampling could favor immediate empiric treatment while diagnostic work continues.

choices.label: Open operative disc/endplate sampling before starting empiric antibiotics
choices.rationale: Sampling before treatment fits the stated stable phase, but no compressive or mechanical finding supplies an initial operative reason over image-guided acquisition.
choices.temptation: Assume tissue diagnosis requires open surgery whenever spinal infection is suspected.
choices.counterfactual: An operative decompression or stabilization indication could make open samples part of the necessary procedure.

choices.label: Empiric antibiotics before obtaining open operative disc/endplate samples
choices.rationale: This combines treatment-first exposure with an open route not justified by the current stability and imaging findings.
choices.temptation: Escalate both antibiotic urgency and procedural invasiveness from the suspected diagnosis without using the actual clinical state.
choices.counterfactual: Sepsis with a separate urgent operative indication would create a different sequence in which treatment and open operative sampling are both required.

nodes.explanation: The decision boundary is specimen acquisition. The untreated, stable patient with negative blood cultures needs etiologic tissue information, and the record gives no initial decompression or stabilization indication. Empiric treatment can begin after specimens are obtained; this question does not require waiting for final cultures or select a drug regimen.
reasoningSteps: Use negative blood cultures and the explicit absence of antimicrobial exposure to identify a remaining need for pretreatment tissue diagnosis.
Use physiological, neurologic and structural stability to select image-guided acquisition before empiric treatment rather than an initial open operation.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Use the appropriate image-guided route but start empiric antibiotics before acquiring tissue.
nodes.decidingObservation: No antimicrobials have actually been given, blood cultures are final negative, and there is no sepsis, new neurologic deficit or structural operative indication.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: New hemodynamic instability would favor immediate empiric treatment rather than waiting for diagnostic tissue acquisition; new neural compression needing decompression would also make open operative sampling relevant.
nodes.deletionTest: The medication record resolves the prior exposure ambiguity. The negative blood cultures establish the etiologic gap. The raw neurological, hemodynamic and structural observations establish the initial route without a 'planned nonsurgical treatment' sentence. The task explicitly separates specimen acquisition from final results.

nodes.task: While continuing bloodstream-infection treatment, which next diagnostic plan best addresses {patientName}'s two spinal sites?

choices.label: Image-guided T8 lesion biopsy for culture and histology
choices.rationale: The bloodstream isolate fits the lumbar disc/endplate pattern, but it does not automatically explain a structurally different thoracic lesion. Tissue at the unresolved site can address infection and mimickers.
choices.temptation: Assume a real bloodstream pathogen supplies the diagnosis for every structural lesion.
choices.counterfactual: If both sites had a compatible disc/endplate pattern with no unexplained separate lesion, routine additional biopsy might add less etiologic information.

choices.label: Image-guided L3-L4 biopsy for culture and histology
choices.rationale: This could resample a site already concordant with the bloodstream evidence while leaving the distinct thoracic process unresolved.
choices.temptation: Apply a biopsy requirement to the conventional-appearing site because it is the symptomatic one.
choices.counterfactual: Atypical lumbar imaging, uncertain bloodstream significance or unresolved lumbar etiology would make lumbar tissue acquisition more relevant.

choices.label: Treatment of both sites with follow-up spinal imaging
choices.rationale: This correctly preserves active bacteremia treatment but assumes the separate lesion shares the lumbar cause without resolving its different structural pattern.
choices.temptation: Generalize the no-routine-biopsy principle from a compatible site to an etiologically discordant site.
choices.counterfactual: Compatible findings at both sites with a sufficiently established cause and no unresolved alternative could support treatment with clinical/imaging reassessment.

nodes.explanation: A convincing blood isolate can remove the need for a routine diagnostic biopsy of a matching spinal infection. That inference is site specific. A distinct lesion with a different structural pattern can merit its own culture and histology while treatment of proven bacteremia continues. Disc preservation does not prove a tumor or exclude infection; it contributes to unresolved concordance.
reasoningSteps: Relate the bloodstream isolate to the compatible lumbar disc/endplate pattern without assuming every spinal lesion has that cause.
Select tissue from the separate unresolved site to discriminate infection from mimicking disease while keeping bacteremia treatment common.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Treat both sites as one bloodstream-seeded process without sampling the discordant lesion.
nodes.decidingObservation: The lumbar site has a compatible contiguous disc/endplate pattern, whereas the separate T8 lesion has a destructive vertebral/pedicle mass pattern with preserved adjacent disc signal.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Replace the discrete T8 lesion with another compatible disc/endplate inflammatory focus and remove the unresolved structural alternative: treatment with reassessment rather than routine additional tissue becomes more defensible.
nodes.deletionTest: The organism and treatment row establish genuine concordance and keep therapy from becoming a distractor. Both site descriptions are needed to compare concordance. Stability removes a separate urgent operative question. Delete the discordant site and the reason for its biopsy disappears.

nodes.task: Alongside urgent specialist assessment, which first investigation best addresses {patientName}'s new neurological findings during treatment of lumbar infection?

choices.label: Urgent contrast MRI of the lumbar spine
choices.rationale: The bilateral motor, perineal and bladder findings localize the new concern to spinal neural structures. MRI can assess the canal and epidural tissues despite systemic improvement.
choices.temptation: Use improving inflammatory markers to downgrade a new neural complication or select a study that answers a different structural question.
choices.counterfactual: If MRI were unavailable or unsafe, another rapid spinal imaging route should not be delayed merely to obtain MRI.

choices.label: Urgent contrast CT of the lumbar spine
choices.rationale: CT provides valuable bony information and can be used when MRI cannot be obtained, but MRI is preferred here for the new neural and epidural question.
choices.temptation: Choose a bone-focused study because vertebral infection is already known, without localizing the new deficit.
choices.counterfactual: A predominantly mechanical deformity question, or inability to obtain MRI promptly, could make CT the relevant immediate study.

choices.label: Urgent nerve conduction and lower-limb EMG
choices.rationale: Physiology may clarify a peripheral deficit, but it is not the first investigation of this bilateral motor, perineal and bladder pattern during spinal infection.
choices.temptation: Treat the new weakness as a peripheral neuropathy while setting aside the sacral findings.
choices.counterfactual: An isolated stable peripheral nerve distribution after spinal compression has been excluded would make electrodiagnostic localization useful.

nodes.explanation: The learner has not been given a new MRI diagnosis. The examination must first be localized and then matched to an investigation suited to the canal and epidural tissues. Falling fever and CRP do not settle a new neural problem. Urgent specialist assessment occurs in parallel; no imaging delay or predetermined decompressive operation is endorsed.
reasoningSteps: Localize the new bilateral motor, perineal and bladder findings to a spinal neural concern rather than a biochemical treatment-response question or isolated peripheral deficit.
Choose MRI for the new canal/epidural question while urgent specialist assessment proceeds.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Choose CT because the established disease involves bone, without identifying that the new care question concerns neural and epidural structures.

nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Replace the neural findings with new load-related pain and suspected deformity but preserved power, perineal sensation and voiding: a bone/alignment study can become relevant rather than canal imaging for new neurologic deterioration.

nodes.task: Which study best clarifies {patientName}'s foot-drop localization before a lumbar intervention is considered?

choices.label: Fibular nerve conduction and needle EMG
choices.rationale: The motor map favors a fibular-territory process over one affecting additional root muscles. EDX can localize the current deficit rather than assume an older MRI finding caused it.
choices.temptation: Separate an imaging abnormality from proof of the current symptomatic lesion.
choices.counterfactual: Predominant plantar-flexion weakness and plantar sensory loss with preserved dorsiflexion would redirect targeted testing toward the tibial territory.

choices.label: Repeat lumbar MRI with foraminal assessment
choices.rationale: The pre-deficit narrowing does not establish the cause of this nerve-territory pattern. Localization is needed before a lumbar intervention.
choices.temptation: Anchor on an existing structural abnormality as the cause of any new leg weakness.
choices.counterfactual: New root-pattern findings, neural red flags or a discordant EDX pattern could justify renewed lumbar imaging.

choices.label: Tibial nerve conduction and needle EMG
choices.rationale: An isolated tibial-focused assessment does not interrogate the main weak dorsiflexion/eversion territory.
choices.temptation: Choose a nearby leg nerve without matching its motor territory.
choices.counterfactual: Plantar-flexion weakness and plantar sensory loss with preserved dorsiflexion could make tibial assessment central.

nodes.explanation: Fit the current motor map before assigning causation to an image. Preserved nonfibular functions and an MRI predating the deficit favor fibular-directed EDX. Postoperative timing alone does not prove an anesthetic or positioning cause.
reasoningSteps: Interpret weak dorsiflexion/eversion alongside preserved inversion and hip abduction.
Apply the old scan provenance to choose physiologic localization before a spine-directed intervention.

nodes.deletionTest: Delete preserved nonfibular functions and the root alternative is less separable. Delete the MRI date and a newly acquired concordant lesion has a different role.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: At the pre-intervention review, the hand clinician has the actual acquisition sheet rather than just the outside report's conclusion.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next study best resolves whether the outside conduction result supports an intervention for {patientName}'s hand symptoms?

answerChoices.label: Temperature-controlled median and control-nerve conduction studies
answerChoices.rationale: The sensory map makes a distal median process plausible, but this isolated absolute measurement is confounded. A controlled comparative acquisition can establish whether focal slowing is real.

answerChoices.label: Needle EMG of cervical paraspinal and proximal arm muscles
answerChoices.rationale: The old foraminal image is a plausible competing explanation, but the current distribution does not supply proximal findings that outweigh the unresolved distal measurement.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound of the median nerve and flexor tendons
answerChoices.rationale: Anatomic ultrasound can address a structural wrist question, but it does not determine whether this temperature-sensitive physiological result demonstrates focal conduction slowing.

decisionNodes.explanation: The symptoms and the acquisition must be interpreted separately. This record supports considering a distal median process but does not yet supply an adequately controlled physiological confirmation. The key corrects this particular confounder; it does not mean every cold-hand study is uninterpretable or that symptoms alone mandate surgery.

items.label: Symptoms
items.value: Intermittent numbness wakes the patient and affects the thumb, index and middle fingers. Grip is limited by the sensory symptoms.

items.label: Acquisition sheet
items.value: The hand skin temperature was 25 C. The report's abnormal conclusion used an isolated absolute median distal latency; no same-distance control-nerve comparison was recorded.

items.label: Competing record
items.value: An older cervical MRI described right foraminal narrowing. Current examination shows preserved proximal arm strength and no radiating neck-to-arm pain.

decisionNodes.stem: Which ultrasound-guided aspiration plan best addresses the unresolved cause of {patientName}'s painful native knee?

answerChoices.label: Lateral suprapatellar entry into the joint
answerChoices.rationale: The first sample does not establish the contents of the joint. This route obtains joint fluid while avoiding the inflamed superficial anterior pocket.

answerChoices.label: Anterior entry through the pocket into the joint
answerChoices.rationale: This would reach the relevant deeper compartment but traverse the overlying inflamed collection, creating an avoidable contamination or inoculation concern.

answerChoices.label: Anterior entry into the prepatellar pocket
answerChoices.rationale: The pocket may need evaluation in its own right, but its fluid will still not represent the separate joint effusion responsible for the unresolved intra-articular concern.

decisionNodes.explanation: A label does not replace specimen provenance. The images show what was sampled; crystals and a negative stain in that fluid do not settle the separate joint question. The new sample must reach the joint through an appropriate route. This sampling decision does not suspend needed systemic treatment or establish that every superficial collection communicates with the joint.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial sampling and treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s current spinal record? In these plans, treatment after sampling means after specimen acquisition, not after final culture results.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided disc/endplate sampling before starting empiric antibiotics
answerChoices.rationale: Stable physiology and neurology allow initial microbiologic/histologic tissue acquisition. Without an operative indication, image-guided sampling is the less invasive initial diagnostic route.

answerChoices.label: Empiric antibiotics before obtaining image-guided disc/endplate samples
answerChoices.rationale: The acquisition route is reasonable, but in this untreated stable record it gives up the opportunity to obtain tissue before antimicrobial exposure.

answerChoices.label: Open operative disc/endplate sampling before starting empiric antibiotics
answerChoices.rationale: Sampling before treatment fits the stated stable phase, but no compressive or mechanical finding supplies an initial operative reason over image-guided acquisition.

answerChoices.label: Empiric antibiotics before obtaining open operative disc/endplate samples
answerChoices.rationale: This combines treatment-first exposure with an open route not justified by the current stability and imaging findings.

decisionNodes.explanation: The decision boundary is specimen acquisition. The untreated, stable patient with negative blood cultures needs etiologic tissue information, and the record gives no initial decompression or stabilization indication. Empiric treatment can begin after specimens are obtained; this question does not require waiting for final cultures or select a drug regimen.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The outside team is already treating the documented bloodstream infection and is deciding whether all spinal findings have the same explanation.
decisionNodes.stem: While continuing bloodstream-infection treatment, which next diagnostic plan best addresses {patientName}'s two spinal sites?

answerChoices.label: Image-guided T8 lesion biopsy for culture and histology
answerChoices.rationale: The bloodstream isolate fits the lumbar disc/endplate pattern, but it does not automatically explain a structurally different thoracic lesion. Tissue at the unresolved site can address infection and mimickers.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided L3-L4 biopsy for culture and histology
answerChoices.rationale: This could resample a site already concordant with the bloodstream evidence while leaving the distinct thoracic process unresolved.

answerChoices.label: Treatment of both sites with follow-up spinal imaging
answerChoices.rationale: This correctly preserves active bacteremia treatment but assumes the separate lesion shares the lumbar cause without resolving its different structural pattern.

decisionNodes.explanation: A convincing blood isolate can remove the need for a routine diagnostic biopsy of a matching spinal infection. That inference is site specific. A distinct lesion with a different structural pattern can merit its own culture and histology while treatment of proven bacteremia continues. Disc preservation does not prove a tumor or exclude infection; it contributes to unresolved concordance.

items.label: Microbiology and shared treatment
items.value: Separate pre-treatment blood-culture sets grew methicillin-susceptible S. aureus. Susceptibility-directed therapy is being administered and continues under every proposed plan.

items.label: Lumbar site
items.value: At L3-L4, MRI shows opposing endplate abnormalities, intervening disc enhancement and adjacent soft-tissue inflammation corresponding to the focal pain.

items.label: Separate thoracic site
items.value: At T8, there is a discrete destructive vertebral/pedicle lesion with a solid adjacent mass; the neighboring discs retain their usual signal. No tissue has been sampled from either site.

items.label: Current state
items.value: The patient is hemodynamically stable without new weakness or bladder/bowel dysfunction.

decisionNodes.stem: Alongside urgent specialist assessment, which first investigation best addresses {patientName}'s new neurological findings during treatment of lumbar infection?

answerChoices.label: Urgent contrast MRI of the lumbar spine
answerChoices.rationale: The bilateral motor, perineal and bladder findings localize the new concern to spinal neural structures. MRI can assess the canal and epidural tissues despite systemic improvement.

answerChoices.label: Urgent contrast CT of the lumbar spine
answerChoices.rationale: CT provides valuable bony information and can be used when MRI cannot be obtained, but MRI is preferred here for the new neural and epidural question.

answerChoices.label: Urgent nerve conduction and lower-limb EMG
answerChoices.rationale: Physiology may clarify a peripheral deficit, but it is not the first investigation of this bilateral motor, perineal and bladder pattern during spinal infection.

decisionNodes.explanation: The learner has not been given a new MRI diagnosis. The examination must first be localized and then matched to an investigation suited to the canal and epidural tissues. Falling fever and CRP do not settle a new neural problem. Urgent specialist assessment occurs in parallel; no imaging delay or predetermined decompressive operation is endorsed.

items.label: New examination
items.value: Both legs have become progressively weaker. Ankle movement and perineal sensation are reduced, and the patient newly cannot empty the bladder.

decisionNodes.stem: Which study best clarifies {patientName}'s foot-drop localization before a lumbar intervention is considered?

answerChoices.label: Fibular nerve conduction and needle EMG
answerChoices.rationale: The motor map favors a fibular-territory process over one affecting additional root muscles. EDX can localize the current deficit rather than assume an older MRI finding caused it.

answerChoices.label: Repeat lumbar MRI with foraminal assessment
answerChoices.rationale: The pre-deficit narrowing does not establish the cause of this nerve-territory pattern. Localization is needed before a lumbar intervention.

answerChoices.label: Tibial nerve conduction and needle EMG
answerChoices.rationale: An isolated tibial-focused assessment does not interrogate the main weak dorsiflexion/eversion territory.

decisionNodes.explanation: Fit the current motor map before assigning causation to an image. Preserved nonfibular functions and an MRI predating the deficit favor fibular-directed EDX. Postoperative timing alone does not prove an anesthetic or positioning cause.

items.value: Dorsiflexion and eversion are weak; inversion and hip abduction remain strong. Sensory loss affects the dorsal foot.

items.label: Clinical course
items.value: The deficit persists; the MRI predates it and no electrodiagnostic localization is available.
