revisionSpecifications.objective: Resolve a technically confounded conduction result before using it to justify a wrist intervention.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: At the pre-intervention review, the hand clinician has the actual acquisition sheet rather than just the outside report's conclusion.
items: Symptoms
Intermittent numbness wakes the patient and affects the thumb, index and middle fingers. Grip is limited by the sensory symptoms.
Acquisition sheet
The hand skin temperature was 25 C. The report's abnormal conclusion used an isolated absolute median distal latency; no same-distance control-nerve comparison was recorded.
Competing record
An older cervical MRI described right foraminal narrowing. Current examination shows preserved proximal arm strength and no radiating neck-to-arm pain.
revisionSpecifications.task: Which next study best resolves whether the outside conduction result supports an intervention for {patientName}'s hand symptoms?
choices: Temperature-controlled median and control-nerve conduction studies
The sensory map makes a distal median process plausible, but this isolated absolute measurement is confounded. A controlled comparative acquisition can establish whether focal slowing is real.
Accept the report's abnormal label as sufficient confirmation for an intervention.
If the available study already contained adequate concordant comparative measurements, this technical repeat would not be the best next step.
Needle EMG of cervical paraspinal and proximal arm muscles
The old foraminal image is a plausible competing explanation, but the current distribution does not supply proximal findings that outweigh the unresolved distal measurement.
Anchor on a structural cervical abnormality while treating the distal study as already validated.
New radiating arm pain and weakness outside distal median muscles would make a proximal localization study relevant.
Ultrasound of the median nerve and flexor tendons
Anatomic ultrasound can address a structural wrist question, but it does not determine whether this temperature-sensitive physiological result demonstrates focal conduction slowing.
Substitute an anatomic image for checking the validity of the physiological evidence being used to justify treatment.
A concordant valid physiological study plus unexplained focal fullness would create a structural imaging question.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: The symptoms and the acquisition must be interpreted separately. This record supports considering a distal median process but does not yet supply an adequately controlled physiological confirmation. The key corrects this particular confounder; it does not mean every cold-hand study is uninterpretable or that symptoms alone mandate surgery.
steps: Localize the sensory complaint while resisting attribution to the older cervical image.
Identify the confounder in an isolated absolute latency and choose an acquisition that resolves it before intervention.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Use the old foraminal MRI to redirect testing without first resolving the technically uncertain distal result.
revisionSpecifications.decider: Only an isolated absolute latency from a cold hand supports the reported distal abnormality; the clinical distribution lacks the proximal findings that would favor the root study.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: Replace the sensory-only distal pattern with radiating neck-to-arm pain and weakness in several nonmedian proximal muscles: the root-directed needle study becomes the relevant localization plan.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: Delete the acquisition details and the reason for a controlled repeat disappears. Delete the distribution and proximal examination and root-directed testing cannot be ranked. The older image creates the actual anchoring competitor. The numeric temperature is a fictional measurement, not an authored diagnostic cutoff.
revisionSpecifications.attack: No option repeats a completed normal target. All options are specific new investigations; the task does not name a nerve segment to copy. The acquisition property is necessary decision information rather than an omitted-test announcement. Warming is not treated as a universal requirement for every valid comparative method.
revisionSpecifications.category: Three next diagnostic studies at the pre-intervention verification stage.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate prediction: the close error is accepting a formally abnormal but confounded report or over-weighting the old cervical image. No hard-item or independent PASS claim.
resolutions: Removed the navigation update and replaced it with receipt of the actual acquisition sheet.
Removed wrist-flexion and splint wording overlap and the explicitly normal ulnar-repeat foil.
The prior study now changes whether its conclusion can be used: cold isolated absolute latency versus controlled comparative evidence.
The alternatives test proximal physiology or local structure, with stated counterfactuals; source scope and comparative-method limitations are explicit.

revisionSpecifications.objective: Prioritize progressive distal median motor loss despite sensory relief and a competing cervical image.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: At a later hand review, sensory relief and motor function have moved in different directions.
items: Observed movement
With the palm flat, the thumb cannot abduct perpendicular to the palm against resistance. The thenar contour has flattened and buttoning has become harder.
Conduction and sampling

Median conduction is selectively slowed across the carpal segment relative to same-distance control nerves, with a reduced thenar motor response. Sampled proximal arm muscles retain normal voluntary recruitment.
Competing trends
A local corticosteroid injection substantially reduced the tingling, but thumb power has continued to fall. An older cervical MRI also describes right foraminal narrowing.
revisionSpecifications.task: Which referral plan should lead treatment of {patientName}'s progressive hand motor loss?
choices: Hand-surgical assessment for carpal tunnel release
Selective distal conduction abnormality and progressive palmar-abduction weakness make the motor course consequential even though tingling improved.
Judge treatment success from sensory relief while overlooking deteriorating motor function.
Improved sensation with stable strength and no progressive wasting could support continued nonsurgical follow-up.
Spine-surgical assessment for cervical root decompression
The cervical image is a real competing record, but it is less concordant with the selective distal physiology and thenar deficit than the hand-level findings.
Attribute all hand weakness to an abnormal cervical image despite more concordant distal evidence.
Weakness extending into nonmedian proximal muscles with root-concordant findings would shift priority toward cervical evaluation.
Hand-therapy review for continued conservative symptom care
Sensory improvement makes this tempting, but continued motor deterioration means symptom relief has not resolved the consequential deficit.
Use improvement in tingling as the sole measure of adequate response.
Sustained symptom improvement with preserved strength and no progressive atrophy would make conservative symptom care more appropriate.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: Palmar abduction is specified so the observed deficit is not confused with thumb extension. The current motor trajectory and focal physiology outweigh sensory improvement and an uncorrelated cervical image for this referral decision. This is an assessment for release, not a rule that an old MRI excludes coexisting root disease.
steps: Interpret the precise motor action and selective conduction pattern as distal median dysfunction rather than thumb-extension or generalized root weakness.
Use progressive motor loss, rather than sensory relief, to prioritize hand-surgical assessment.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Continue conservative symptom care because the tingling improved after injection.
revisionSpecifications.decider: Thumb palmar-abduction power and thenar bulk continue to decline despite improved sensory symptoms, with concordant focal distal physiology.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: Keep the sensory improvement but replace the declining power and wasting with preserved, stable thenar function: continued conservative symptom care becomes reasonable instead of escalation for progressive motor loss.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: The movement direction prevents ambiguity with extension or radial abduction. The focal comparative physiology and proximal sampling distinguish the cervical competitor. Removing the differing motor and sensory trends removes the management conflict. Neither conservative option is a verbatim failed repeat.
revisionSpecifications.attack: All choices are named referral plans with comparable scope. Removed the two 'another failed treatment' distractors. The hand and cervical pathways each have a real supplied reason; the key requires reconciling motor decline with sensory relief, not matching the word urgent.
revisionSpecifications.category: Three current referral and management pathways for the hand deficit.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate prediction: sensory improvement and the old cervical image create competing errors. Objective motor decline remains visible; urgency is not concealed for difficulty.
resolutions: Specified palmar abduction perpendicular to the plane of the palm, not an ambiguous thumb lift.
Removed two explicitly failed repeat-treatment options; sensory relief now makes conservative care a credible nearest competitor.
Added a cervical-image competitor but supplied raw focal conduction and precise motor findings to determine the more concordant referral.
Feedback limits the conclusion to assessment and explicitly preserves the possibility of coexisting proximal disease.

revisionSpecifications.objective: Recognize when an apparent elbow neuropathy cannot explain a wider neurologic pattern and redirect the next investigation.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: At reassessment after a nonorthopedic operation, the patient's hand difficulty has extended beyond the initially investigated right elbow territory.
items: Initial record
Right little/ring-finger tingling began after the operation. An outside study found mild focal slowing across the elbow, and protective positioning reduced that tingling.
Current hand findings
Fine finger movements are now slow in both hands, including thumb-index tasks; the patient drops small objects despite the sensory improvement.
Current walking examination
Tandem walking is unsteady. Both knee reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus; lower-limb power had previously been recorded as normal.
revisionSpecifications.task: Which investigation should lead evaluation of {patientName}'s worsening hand function and walking difficulty?
choices: Bilateral hand dysfunction plus upper motor neuron and gait findings cannot be explained by the focal elbow result; cervical cord assessment addresses the broader pattern.
Let a genuine mild elbow abnormality explain every later symptom.
A purely unilateral ulnar sensory/motor deficit without gait or upper motor neuron findings would keep the local nerve pathway in the foreground.
MRI of the right brachial plexus
A postoperative arm problem can prompt plexus imaging, but a unilateral plexus lesion does not account for the bilateral hand and leg findings.
Infer a larger peripheral injury from the postoperative timing without localizing the whole examination.
Weakness across several nerves in one arm with a matching peripheral distribution and no leg signs would make plexus assessment more relevant.
The local study and initial paresthesia make this plausible, but a local elbow image will not resolve the new bilateral and lower-limb pattern.
Keep escalating local imaging because the first abnormal test was at the elbow.
Persistent focal elbow symptoms with a local mass or other unresolved structural finding would make elbow imaging a relevant next inquiry.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: The initial focal finding need not be false to be insufficient. The resident must localize the newly broader examination before choosing imaging: hand dysfunction with gait and upper motor neuron findings raises a cervical cord concern. No diagnosis or operative technique is established before imaging.
steps: Determine that the distribution and long-tract findings extend beyond an isolated postoperative ulnar or unilateral plexus deficit.
Select cervical MRI to assess the cord rather than continue local arm imaging.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Continue elbow imaging because an earlier physiological abnormality genuinely involved that region.
revisionSpecifications.decider: New bilateral dexterity impairment is accompanied by gait dysfunction, brisk leg reflexes and ankle clonus.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: Replace the bilateral hand and leg findings with persistent unilateral little/ring-finger symptoms and a focal elbow fullness: local elbow imaging becomes relevant, and the basis for cervical cord priority disappears.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: The initial genuine focal result creates the anchoring error and the actual sensory response prevents calling it a failed local treatment. Bilateral hand involvement and the walking/reflex findings establish a different localization. Removing those findings eliminates the reason to prioritize cervical over peripheral imaging.
revisionSpecifications.attack: All three alternatives are new MRI investigations, with the same timing profile and no unique urgency word. The record gives raw examination findings rather than a diagnosis label. No option repeats an explicitly normal protocol and no lone median foil remains.
revisionSpecifications.category: Three regional MRI investigations at the same current localization stage.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate prediction: a true local abnormality competes with a new central distribution. The question does not require short-segment technical acquisition recall.
resolutions: Replaced nonspecific needle 'abnormalities' and technical inching recall with directly observed distribution, gait and reflex findings.
Removed the already-normal same-span repeat and the weak median-wrist foil; all options are plausible regional MRI studies.
The postoperative elbow finding is genuine but insufficient, so the discordance changes the clinical investigation.
Scope is nontraumatic compression recognition and peripheral-versus-cord attribution, with no traumatic-spine or operative-family objective.

revisionSpecifications.objective: Choose the side and need for surgical assessment from motor trajectory rather than bilateral sonographic nerve mobility.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: During follow-up, the tingling has improved but right-hand motor function has deteriorated.
items: Clinical trend
Protective elbow positioning has reduced right little/ring-finger tingling. Right finger spreading is progressively weaker and the first dorsal interosseous contour is flattening.
Paired examination and studies
Right elbow conduction is focally slowed with reduced intrinsic motor response and spontaneous activity in the first dorsal interosseous. Left hand strength, sensation and conduction remain normal.
Bilateral ultrasound
The ulnar nerve moves anterior to the medial epicondyle during flexion on each side. The left arm has no symptoms.
revisionSpecifications.task: Which management plan best fits {patientName}'s current elbow and hand findings?
choices: Refer for right cubital-tunnel surgical assessment
The right motor trajectory and concordant physiology justify escalation despite sensory improvement; bilateral mobility does not establish bilateral symptomatic disease.
Choose treatment intensity and side from an image instead of the functional deficit.
If right strength and function were preserved and symptoms continued to settle, protective care could remain appropriate.
Continue protective elbow care with clinical follow-up
This fits the sensory improvement but underweights progressive objective right motor loss and muscle wasting.
Define success by less tingling while ignoring worsening intrinsic function.
Improving paresthesia with stable normal power and no progressive muscle loss would favor continued protective care.
Refer for bilateral cubital-tunnel surgical assessment
The ultrasound shows mobility on both sides, but the left side has no clinical or physiological neuropathy to justify the same escalation.
Treat bilateral sonographic mobility as bilateral disease requiring equivalent intervention.
Bilateral concordant symptoms, objective deficits and nonresponse would justify assessing both sides rather than inferring disease from mobility alone.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: The current decision concerns progressive right motor dysfunction, not obtaining a dynamic image. Less tingling does not reverse the recorded weakness. The asymptomatic left arm demonstrates why a mobility finding must be clinically correlated; the draft does not choose decompression versus transposition or declare mobility harmless in every patient.
steps: Reconcile improving sensory symptoms with worsening right intrinsic motor function and focal physiology.
Escalate the affected side while recognizing that the same ultrasound movement on an asymptomatic side does not establish equal disease.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Continue protective care because paresthesia is improving, or extend the referral bilaterally because the images look alike.
revisionSpecifications.decider: Only the right side has progressive weakness, wasting and concordant physiological dysfunction; the left mobility finding lacks symptoms or functional loss.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: If both sides instead had preserved power and normal physiology with steadily settling symptoms, continued protective care would replace surgical escalation. If both sides developed concordant deficits, bilateral assessment could become reasonable.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: Removing the actual sensory response eliminates the conservative competitor. Removing motor trend and physiology eliminates the reason to escalate. Removing the left comparison makes the bilateral imaging-based error impossible to assess. The motion finding no longer uniquely matches a proposed acquisition.
revisionSpecifications.attack: There is no named unperformed acquisition or dynamic-versus-static word match. All choices are present management plans. The closest alternative is continued protective care based on a real response; the side-selection error requires interpreting a bilateral structural finding against unequal clinical evidence.
revisionSpecifications.category: Three current management plans differing in escalation and clinically affected side.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate prediction: discordant sensory/motor trends and a bilateral image with unilateral disease. No claim that the item is hard merely because it is a later node.
resolutions: Removed the missing-flexion-acquisition sentence, snap-to-dynamic match and both static imaging distractors.
Changed the scored objective to a practical motor-progression and side-selection decision.
Supplied an actual conservative response plus discordant motor decline, and a clinically normal opposite side to make image correlation consequential.
Did not rank operative techniques or claim that sonographic mobility alone proves causation.

revisionSpecifications.objective: Use recovery evidence after postoperative trapezius dysfunction to choose continued rehabilitation rather than premature reconstruction.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: At follow-up after initial peripheral-nerve assessment, serial function and repeat muscle sampling are available.
items: Initial postoperative findings

After an outside posterior-triangle lymph-node excision, the right shoulder rested lower, shrug was weak and overhead reach was limited. Initial trapezius sampling showed greatly reduced voluntary recruitment.
Serial function
With supervised rehabilitation, overhead reach and resisted shrug have improved on successive examinations. The scapular outline remains asymmetric.
Repeat sampling
The same trapezius regions now show new voluntary motor units with greater recruitment than on the baseline study.
revisionSpecifications.task: Which current management plan best fits {patientName}'s postoperative shoulder trajectory?
choices: Continue supervised shoulder rehabilitation and reassessment
Actual functional recovery and returning recruitment support ongoing conservative care despite persistent visible asymmetry.
Treat a persistent scapular outline as proof that the recovery pathway has failed.
Absent improvement or new deterioration would prompt renewed peripheral-nerve surgical evaluation rather than assuming recovery.
The operation and initial deficit make this a credible pathway, but current recovery and new recruitment do not support escalation on appearance alone.
Infer a repair indication from the operative location without weighing evidence of recovery.
Known transection, deterioration or a persistently nonrecovering lesion would change the specialist exploration question.
A fixed persistent deficit may eventually create a reconstruction question, but this record documents improving neural and functional performance.
Treat residual winging during recovery as an established nonrecovering functional deficit.
A lasting disabling nonrecovering deficit after specialist evaluation and rehabilitation could make reconstructive assessment relevant.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: The operation and initial movement localize the problem, but they do not establish transection or a reconstruction deadline. Returning voluntary recruitment together with improving function changes the next plan. The evidence supports a recovery principle; Melissa must confirm this exact pathway, and no fixed repair window is authored.
steps: Interpret returning motor-unit recruitment together with serial functional improvement as recovery rather than equating visible asymmetry with treatment failure.
Choose continued supervised rehabilitation instead of an unsupported immediate exploration or reconstruction plan.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Request exploration because the nerve was at risk during neck surgery and the scapular outline is still abnormal.
revisionSpecifications.decider: Both serial function and recruitment have improved in the same affected muscle despite residual asymmetry.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: Replace the improving function and returning recruitment with worsening function and persistently absent recruitment: renewed peripheral-nerve surgical assessment becomes appropriate, without automatically proving transection or selecting a repair technique.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: The initial operation and muscle findings establish the postoperative nerve territory. The serial measurements and matched repeat sampling change the care phase. Visible residual asymmetry creates the credible conflicting signal. Deleting the recovery data would leave exploration versus continued rehabilitation unresolved.
revisionSpecifications.attack: Removed the forward-push negative and repeat-normal deltoid option. No unsampled-muscle novelty remains. All choices are specific current management pathways; interpreting the actual recovery data is necessary before choosing among them.
revisionSpecifications.category: Three current rehabilitation, exploration or reconstruction pathways.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate prediction with an evidence limitation: residual deformity competes with genuine recovery. Older advisory support is disclosed and no current operative timing is asserted.
resolutions: Replaced one-step muscle-target recall with a recovery-versus-persistent-appearance care decision.
Removed the negative that disposed of serratus and the normal-deltoid repeat foil.
Actual serial function and new recruitment now alter the choice; the baseline cannot be deleted without losing the comparison.
Kept nerve-territory anatomy while explicitly declining to infer transection or an exact exploration deadline; single older advisory limitation retained.

revisionSpecifications.objective: Interpret the actual aspirate compartment and choose a safe route to sample an unresolved native-joint concern.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: The outside team has the procedure images behind the specimen labeled 'knee aspirate' and must decide how to obtain the next local sample.
items: Fluid report
The submitted fluid contained monosodium urate crystals and neutrophils; no organisms were seen on Gram stain, and culture was pending.
Procedure images
The saved needle tip ends in a fluid pocket between the skin and patella. A separate suprapatellar joint effusion is visible.
Current examination
Fever and marked pain through passive knee motion persist. Redness and the superficial pocket cover the anterior patella; skin over the lateral suprapatellar recess is intact.
revisionSpecifications.task: Which ultrasound-guided aspiration plan best addresses the unresolved cause of {patientName}'s painful native knee?
choices: Lateral suprapatellar entry into the joint
The first sample does not establish the contents of the joint. This route obtains joint fluid while avoiding the inflamed superficial anterior pocket.
Accept a specimen label and its crystals as proof that the intra-articular compartment has been evaluated.
If an adequate intra-articular sample already existed and there were no remaining joint concern, repeating joint aspiration would require a new reason.
Anterior entry through the pocket into the joint
This would reach the relevant deeper compartment but traverse the overlying inflamed collection, creating an avoidable contamination or inoculation concern.
Correct the target compartment without considering the access route.
An anterior approach through uninflamed tissue without an intervening collection can be an acceptable joint access route.
Anterior entry into the prepatellar pocket
The pocket may need evaluation in its own right, but its fluid will still not represent the separate joint effusion responsible for the unresolved intra-articular concern.
Treat the superficial crystal-containing collection as the complete explanation for the painful knee.
A purely superficial process without a joint effusion or pain on passive joint motion would make the superficial pocket the relevant local target.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: A label does not replace specimen provenance. The images show what was sampled; crystals and a negative stain in that fluid do not settle the separate joint question. The new sample must reach the joint through an appropriate route. This sampling decision does not suspend needed systemic treatment or establish that every superficial collection communicates with the joint.
steps: Infer from needle position that the crystal-containing sample did not represent the separate joint effusion, leaving the joint concern unresolved.
Choose access to the joint that avoids traversing the inflamed superficial collection.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Use an anterior route that reaches the joint but crosses the superficial pocket.
revisionSpecifications.decider: The documented needle tip is superficial to the patella, while a separate joint effusion and passive-motion pain remain; the anterior route crosses the inflamed pocket.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: If the anterior skin and path were uninflamed with no intervening collection, anterior entry could be reasonable. If the painful process were confined to a superficial pocket without effusion or passive-motion pain, the pocket would become the local aspiration target.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: Delete the actual tip location and the first aspirate's scope cannot be judged. Delete the separate effusion and passive-motion pain and the need for joint sampling weakens. Delete the overlying collection and skin findings and the lateral-versus-anterior route cannot be ranked. The crystal result remains a genuine misleading attribution, not a diagnosis label.
revisionSpecifications.attack: All options are ultrasound-guided aspiration routes, with identical timing metadata. None abandons antibiotics or offers steroid injection. The closest competitor reaches the same joint, so the learner must interpret both sample provenance and access anatomy rather than choose the only infection-preserving treatment.
revisionSpecifications.category: Three local aspiration routes at the same diagnostic sampling stage.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate prediction: two linked anatomy/provenance decisions replace the single crystals-do-not-exclude-infection rule. No easy-item exception or independent PASS is claimed.
resolutions: Removed colchicine/steroid treatment-replacement foils and kept the decision at a single local sampling stage.
New procedure images show that the reported crystals came from a different compartment; the label cannot establish joint sampling adequacy.
Added actual skin/path observations that make the nearest competing joint-entry route less appropriate, supported by SANJO aspiration guidance.
Crystals and negative Gram stain are limited to the sampled fluid; no statement suspends needed antimicrobial or source-control care.

revisionSpecifications.objective: Select immediate local compression assessment from evolving postoperative limb findings after block resolution.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: The clinic review reaches the outside postoperative assessment after the repeat knee washout; the question concerns what that hospital team needed to assess immediately.
items: Block and motor course
The regional block had resolved with initially documented ankle movement. Later examinations showed progressively weaker ankle dorsiflexion and toe movement.
Local findings
Deep calf pain rose despite analgesia. The calf became swollen and firm, and passive toe movement markedly increased pain.
Perfusion
The foot remained warm with palpable pedal pulses.
revisionSpecifications.task: Which immediate evaluation should lead the outside team's response to {patientName}'s worsening postoperative leg findings?
choices: Immediate surgical assessment of calf compartments
The progressive deep pain, stretch pain, firmness and evolving motor deficit require bedside assessment for treatable local pressure despite preserved pulses.
Use a warm foot and pulses to exclude a pressure problem or route the weakness directly to delayed nerve testing.
Soft painless compartments with an isolated stable nerve-territory deficit would favor a peripheral-nerve localization assessment.
Immediate venous assessment with leg duplex ultrasound
Postoperative swelling makes venous thrombosis a credible concern, but duplex does not resolve the combined stretch pain, firmness and worsening motor deficit that need direct compartment assessment.
Attribute painful postoperative swelling to venous obstruction while underweighting the evolving local neuromuscular findings.
Swelling and venous tenderness without compartment firmness, stretch pain or neurologic progression would make venous investigation more appropriate.
Progressive weakness deserves specialist attention, but physiology is not the first way to exclude a surgically treatable local pressure problem in this painful swollen limb.
Assume every post-block motor deficit should first be classified by nerve conduction or EMG.
A persisting localized deficit after reversible compression is excluded, with a soft painless limb, would make electrodiagnostic localization useful.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: The deficit appeared after block resolution and is progressing with local pain and swelling. Palpable pulses assess arterial flow but do not exclude a compartment pressure problem. Surgical bedside assessment must address reversible compression; pressure measurement may assist when indicated. The draft neither diagnoses a specific mechanism from timing nor substitutes consultation for examining the limb.
steps: Interpret the serial motor loss with local stretch pain and firmness as a possible treatable pressure complication rather than residual block or an isolated physiological nerve problem.
Prioritize immediate compartment-focused surgical assessment over other urgent but less relevant investigations.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Obtain venous duplex first because postoperative pain and swelling suggest thrombosis.
revisionSpecifications.decider: Progressive motor loss occurs with a firm calf and pain on passive stretch, despite a warm foot and palpable pulses.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: Replace the firm, stretch-painful limb and progressive motor deficit with soft compartments, normal power and predominantly venous swelling/tenderness: urgent venous duplex becomes the more relevant investigation.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: Block resolution and initially present movement establish a new progressive deficit. Local pain, stretch pain and firmness select the assessment pathway; preserved pulses create a real false-reassurance competitor. The old early-normal EDX detail was removed because it did not change urgency or test ranking. All proposed paths remain immediate.
revisionSpecifications.attack: Every option explicitly says immediate and offers an actual evaluation, so urgency wording cannot select the key. No routine-follow-up or delay foil remains. Raw local findings, not a supplied compartment diagnosis, must determine the pathway.
revisionSpecifications.category: Three immediate postoperative limb evaluation pathways.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate prediction: urgent venous and neural investigations are plausible, but the local pattern selects direct compartment assessment. Essential red flags stay visible.
resolutions: Replaced vague urgent consultation with immediate surgical compartment assessment tied to actual pain, firmness, passive-stretch and motor findings.
Kept block resolution and serial progression; removed the normal early EDX detail after failing the deletion test.
All options are urgent evaluations, removing the unique-urgent-versus-routine cue.
Preserved pulses are explicitly not an exclusion; no pressure cutoff, automatic fasciotomy or specific anesthetic/surgical mechanism is inferred.

revisionSpecifications.objective: Choose the initial tissue-acquisition route and empiric-treatment boundary in a stable culture-negative spinal-infection evaluation.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: The outside team has completed blood-culture incubation, has not administered antimicrobials and is choosing the first tissue-sampling and treatment sequence.
items: MRI observations

Opposing lumbar endplate marrow abnormalities and intervening disc enhancement accompany adjacent paraspinal inflammation. There is no epidural collection, neural compression or destructive deformity.
Microbiology and medication record
Blood cultures collected at the initial evaluation have finalized without growth. No antimicrobial dose has been administered since collection.
Current clinical state
Blood pressure and perfusion are normal; the patient is alert. Leg power, sensation and bladder/bowel function remain unchanged. No spinal procedure has yet been performed.
revisionSpecifications.task: Which initial sampling and treatment sequence best fits {patientName}'s current spinal record? In these plans, treatment after sampling means after specimen acquisition, not after final culture results.
choices: Image-guided disc/endplate sampling before starting empiric antibiotics
Stable physiology and neurology allow initial microbiologic/histologic tissue acquisition. Without an operative indication, image-guided sampling is the less invasive initial diagnostic route.
Treat acquisition and final laboratory results as the same boundary or infer an operation from the MRI label.
New sepsis or neurologic deterioration would change whether treatment and operative assessment can wait for this diagnostic sequence.
Empiric antibiotics before obtaining image-guided disc/endplate samples
The acquisition route is reasonable, but in this untreated stable record it gives up the opportunity to obtain tissue before antimicrobial exposure.
Treat MRI suspicion as requiring antimicrobial administration before available diagnostic sampling in every stable patient.
Hemodynamic instability or an unsafe delay to sampling could favor immediate empiric treatment while diagnostic work continues.
Open operative disc/endplate sampling before starting empiric antibiotics
Sampling before treatment fits the stated stable phase, but no compressive or mechanical finding supplies an initial operative reason over image-guided acquisition.
Assume tissue diagnosis requires open surgery whenever spinal infection is suspected.
An operative decompression or stabilization indication could make open samples part of the necessary procedure.
Empiric antibiotics before obtaining open operative disc/endplate samples

Escalate both antibiotic urgency and procedural invasiveness from the suspected diagnosis without using the actual clinical state.
Sepsis with a separate urgent operative indication would create a different sequence in which treatment and open operative sampling are both required.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: The decision boundary is specimen acquisition. The untreated, stable patient with negative blood cultures needs etiologic tissue information, and the record gives no initial decompression or stabilization indication. Empiric treatment can begin after specimens are obtained; this question does not require waiting for final cultures or select a drug regimen.
steps: Use negative blood cultures and the explicit absence of antimicrobial exposure to identify a remaining need for pretreatment tissue diagnosis.
Use physiological, neurologic and structural stability to select image-guided acquisition before empiric treatment rather than an initial open operation.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Use the appropriate image-guided route but start empiric antibiotics before acquiring tissue.
revisionSpecifications.decider: No antimicrobials have actually been given, blood cultures are final negative, and there is no sepsis, new neurologic deficit or structural operative indication.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: New hemodynamic instability would favor immediate empiric treatment rather than waiting for diagnostic tissue acquisition; new neural compression needing decompression would also make open operative sampling relevant.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: The medication record resolves the prior exposure ambiguity. The negative blood cultures establish the etiologic gap. The raw neurological, hemodynamic and structural observations establish the initial route without a 'planned nonsurgical treatment' sentence. The task explicitly separates specimen acquisition from final results.
revisionSpecifications.attack: Removed the preannounced nonsurgical plan. The four options balance acquisition route and treatment order: each route and each timing appears twice, so component majority or novelty cannot identify the key. Labels have the same specificity and differ in consequential sequence, not explanatory qualifications.
revisionSpecifications.category: Four initial acquisition-and-treatment sequences using a balanced route-by-order comparison.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate prediction, consistent with the prior reviewer: a plausible treatment-first approach competes with initial tissue acquisition. No artificial hard label or fixed waiting period.
resolutions: Explicitly states that no antimicrobial dose has been given since the blood cultures were collected.
Defines 'after sampling' as after specimen acquisition, not final culture results.
Removed 'specialists planned nonsurgical treatment'; actual stability and imaging determine route.
Balanced four options remove component-frequency convergence while retaining distinct route/order decisions; no drug regimen or fixed delay is invented.

revisionSpecifications.objective: Apply bloodstream concordance to the matching spinal site while recognizing that a separate discordant lesion may need its own tissue diagnosis.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: The outside team is already treating the documented bloodstream infection and is deciding whether all spinal findings have the same explanation.
items: Microbiology and shared treatment
Separate pre-treatment blood-culture sets grew methicillin-susceptible S. aureus. Susceptibility-directed therapy is being administered and continues under every proposed plan.
Lumbar site
At L3-L4, MRI shows opposing endplate abnormalities, intervening disc enhancement and adjacent soft-tissue inflammation corresponding to the focal pain.
Separate thoracic site
At T8, there is a discrete destructive vertebral/pedicle lesion with a solid adjacent mass; the neighboring discs retain their usual signal. No tissue has been sampled from either site.
Current state
The patient is hemodynamically stable without new weakness or bladder/bowel dysfunction.
revisionSpecifications.task: While continuing bloodstream-infection treatment, which next diagnostic plan best addresses {patientName}'s two spinal sites?
choices: Image-guided T8 lesion biopsy for culture and histology

The bloodstream isolate fits the lumbar disc/endplate pattern, but it does not automatically explain a structurally different thoracic lesion. Tissue at the unresolved site can address infection and mimickers.
Assume a real bloodstream pathogen supplies the diagnosis for every structural lesion.
If both sites had a compatible disc/endplate pattern with no unexplained separate lesion, routine additional biopsy might add less etiologic information.
Image-guided L3-L4 biopsy for culture and histology
This could resample a site already concordant with the bloodstream evidence while leaving the distinct thoracic process unresolved.
Apply a biopsy requirement to the conventional-appearing site because it is the symptomatic one.
Atypical lumbar imaging, uncertain bloodstream significance or unresolved lumbar etiology would make lumbar tissue acquisition more relevant.
Treatment of both sites with follow-up spinal imaging
This correctly preserves active bacteremia treatment but assumes the separate lesion shares the lumbar cause without resolving its different structural pattern.
Generalize the no-routine-biopsy principle from a compatible site to an etiologically discordant site.
Compatible findings at both sites with a sufficiently established cause and no unresolved alternative could support treatment with clinical/imaging reassessment.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: A convincing blood isolate can remove the need for a routine diagnostic biopsy of a matching spinal infection. That inference is site specific. A distinct lesion with a different structural pattern can merit its own culture and histology while treatment of proven bacteremia continues. Disc preservation does not prove a tumor or exclude infection; it contributes to unresolved concordance.
steps: Relate the bloodstream isolate to the compatible lumbar disc/endplate pattern without assuming every spinal lesion has that cause.
Select tissue from the separate unresolved site to discriminate infection from mimicking disease while keeping bacteremia treatment common.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Treat both sites as one bloodstream-seeded process without sampling the discordant lesion.
revisionSpecifications.decider: The lumbar site has a compatible contiguous disc/endplate pattern, whereas the separate T8 lesion has a destructive vertebral/pedicle mass pattern with preserved adjacent disc signal.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: Replace the discrete T8 lesion with another compatible disc/endplate inflammatory focus and remove the unresolved structural alternative: treatment with reassessment rather than routine additional tissue becomes more defensible.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: The organism and treatment row establish genuine concordance and keep therapy from becoming a distractor. Both site descriptions are needed to compare concordance. Stability removes a separate urgent operative question. Delete the discordant site and the reason for its biopsy disappears.
revisionSpecifications.attack: Uses a plain next-plan task. All options continue the same active treatment; none advertises ignoring the supplied organism or delaying bacteremia care. The two biopsy targets and treatment-with-imaging plan represent different actual diagnostic strategies, not duplicate treatment-deferral choices.
revisionSpecifications.category: Three next diagnostic strategies while an established infection is treated.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate/hard prediction from site-specific concordance and a credible unifying-diagnosis error. Exact target and comparative plan remain subject to Melissa's clinical review.
resolutions: Replaced the abstract etiologic-plan wording with a plain next diagnostic plan.
Made active susceptibility-directed bacteremia treatment common to every choice.
Added a genuine discordant-site interpretation that changes whether and where biopsy contributes.
Removed duplicate biopsy-result deferrals and unsupported open sampling; no claim that every positive culture or preserved disc establishes a universal diagnosis.

revisionSpecifications.objective: Localize new neurologic deterioration during treated spinal infection and select urgent canal imaging before a cause is supplied.
revisionSpecifications.currentUpdate: During treatment at the outside hospital, a new neurological change has triggered urgent spine-team assessment; the first investigation must now be selected.
items: Earlier documented state
The patient was walking and emptying the bladder normally when treatment for the lumbar infection began.
Treatment trajectory
Susceptibility-directed antibiotics have reduced fever and CRP. The last imaging was obtained before the new neurological findings.
New examination
Both legs have become progressively weaker. Ankle movement and perineal sensation are reduced, and the patient newly cannot empty the bladder.
revisionSpecifications.task: Alongside urgent specialist assessment, which first investigation best addresses {patientName}'s new neurological findings during treatment of lumbar infection?
choices: Urgent contrast MRI of the lumbar spine
The bilateral motor, perineal and bladder findings localize the new concern to spinal neural structures. MRI can assess the canal and epidural tissues despite systemic improvement.
Use improving inflammatory markers to downgrade a new neural complication or select a study that answers a different structural question.
If MRI were unavailable or unsafe, another rapid spinal imaging route should not be delayed merely to obtain MRI.
Urgent contrast CT of the lumbar spine
CT provides valuable bony information and can be used when MRI cannot be obtained, but MRI is preferred here for the new neural and epidural question.
Choose a bone-focused study because vertebral infection is already known, without localizing the new deficit.
A predominantly mechanical deformity question, or inability to obtain MRI promptly, could make CT the relevant immediate study.
Urgent nerve conduction and lower-limb EMG
Physiology may clarify a peripheral deficit, but it is not the first investigation of this bilateral motor, perineal and bladder pattern during spinal infection.
Treat the new weakness as a peripheral neuropathy while setting aside the sacral findings.
An isolated stable peripheral nerve distribution after spinal compression has been excluded would make electrodiagnostic localization useful.
revisionSpecifications.explanation: The learner has not been given a new MRI diagnosis. The examination must first be localized and then matched to an investigation suited to the canal and epidural tissues. Falling fever and CRP do not settle a new neural problem. Urgent specialist assessment occurs in parallel; no imaging delay or predetermined decompressive operation is endorsed.
steps: Localize the new bilateral motor, perineal and bladder findings to a spinal neural concern rather than a biochemical treatment-response question or isolated peripheral deficit.
Choose MRI for the new canal/epidural question while urgent specialist assessment proceeds.
revisionSpecifications.nearest: Choose CT because the established disease involves bone, without identifying that the new care question concerns neural and epidural structures.
revisionSpecifications.decider: The new bilateral weakness, perineal sensory change and urinary retention appeared after previously normal walking/voiding; no current image explains them.
revisionSpecifications.counterfactual: Replace the neural findings with new load-related pain and suspected deformity but preserved power, perineal sensation and voiding: a bone/alignment study can become relevant rather than canal imaging for new neurologic deterioration.
revisionSpecifications.deletion: The baseline proves a new change; the treatment trend creates a genuine false-reassurance signal. Bilateral and sacral findings establish the localization. The chronology prevents treating the old scan as a current explanation. The supplied 'compression' MRI interpretation and its matching decompression answer were removed.
revisionSpecifications.attack: All choices are urgent investigations, so the adjective does not select the answer. No option merely broadens known-active treatment or resamples microbiology. The record supplies raw examination findings and imaging chronology, not the compressive diagnosis or named operation.
revisionSpecifications.category: Three urgent diagnostic investigations while specialist assessment proceeds.
revisionSpecifications.difficulty: Moderate prediction: the two decisions are neural localization and modality suited to that question. Emergency findings remain explicit; the item is not called difficult solely because CRP improved.
resolutions: Removed the MRI statement that already supplied compression and the matching decompression option.
Preserved progression, bilateral weakness, new retention and the prior-normal baseline; added perineal findings as constructed localization data.
Compared three urgent investigations, keeping specialist assessment common rather than uniquely urgent.
Explained why improved systemic markers do not resolve the new neural problem, without inventing a diagnosis or operation before imaging.
